title: Design a URL Shortener
followUps: How do you generate short codes so that two writers never collide? Compare a hash-based approach with a counter- or range-based approach.
Your read traffic is 100x your write traffic. Walk me through exactly what happens on a redirect, and where the cache sits.
How would you support custom aliases and link expiration?
A single link goes viral and receives 1M requests per second. What breaks first, and how do you handle it?
How would you add click analytics without slowing down the redirect path?

interviewer.approach: Strong answers: clarify functional (shorten, redirect, optional custom alias, expiry, analytics) and non-functional requirements (low-latency redirects, high availability, read-heavy). Estimate scale. Define APIs (POST /urls, GET /{code} -> 301/302). Data model: code -> long URL, owner, created, expires. ID generation: base62 of a unique counter (distributed via ranges from a coordinator such as ZooKeeper or a DB sequence) or hashing with collision checks; 7 base62 characters ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. Storage: key-value store (DynamoDB/Cassandra) or sharded SQL. Cache hot codes (Redis) in front of the DB plus CDN at the edge. 301 vs 302 tradeoff (cacheability vs analytics). Analytics asynchronous via a queue/log (Kafka) into an OLAP store. Rate limiting and abuse prevention.
hints: Before drawing boxes: what are the core operations, and what is the read/write ratio?
Try a quick estimate: how many new URLs per day, how much storage over 5 years, and how many redirects per second at peak?
How long does a short code need to be? How many codes can 7 base62 characters represent?
The redirect path is the hot path. What can you put in front of the database?
pitfalls: Jumping into components without clarifying requirements or scale.
Hashing the URL and truncating without handling collisions.
A single global counter that becomes a bottleneck or single point of failure.
Doing analytics writes synchronously on the redirect path.
facts: Read:write ratio is about 100:1 (roughly 10B redirects per day).
URLs are kept for 5 years by default unless the user sets an expiration.
Short codes should be as short as reasonably possible and not trivially guessable in sequence (nice to have).
Custom aliases are a nice-to-have; analytics (click counts per link) is required but may lag by a few minutes.
deepDives: Cache strategy and eviction for hot links
